articles.title: Guardrails, prompt injection and AI security
articles.concept: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted content attempts to redirect application behavior. It is a trust-boundary problem, including indirect instructions hidden in retrieved documents or tool results.
articles.mechanism: Map trusted instructions, user input, retrieved evidence, tools, and credentials separately. Enforce authorization in application code, validate tool arguments, restrict network access, and minimize privileges. Use detection and content screening as additional controls, then test complete attack paths and sensitive side effects rather than relying on a single safety prompt.
articles.boundary: No prompt-only defense guarantees protection. Sanitizing text does not replace least privilege and server-side authorization.
articles.example: A malicious document asks a support agent to send customer records to an external address; the tool policy blocks the action.
articles.application: Tool-connected enterprise assistants exposed to untrusted documents.

articles.title: Responsible AI, privacy and human oversight
articles.concept: Responsible deployment requires understanding affected users, sensitive data, failure consequences, and appropriate human control. Average quality metrics can hide unequal or harmful outcomes.
articles.mechanism: Document intended use and exclusions, minimize collected data, define retention and access, and evaluate relevant user and language segments. Provide an escalation route for uncertain or consequential outputs. Review data provenance and consent before training or logging, and keep operational evidence sufficient for investigation without retaining unnecessary personal information.
articles.boundary: Removing names does not guarantee anonymization. Technical controls support policy obligations but do not replace qualified review of applicable requirements.
articles.example: A hiring-support prototype tests language and accessibility differences and leaves consequential decisions to accountable reviewers.
articles.application: GenAI systems handling personal data or decisions affecting people.

articles.title: LLMOps, observability and controlled releases
articles.concept: LLMOps manages the versions and operational behavior of model-powered applications. Model, prompt, retriever, corpus, and tool changes can each alter outcomes.
articles.mechanism: Attach version identifiers and request correlation IDs to traces. Monitor quality samples, error rates, token usage, latency stages, and retrieval health. Compare releases on fixed evaluation sets and controlled traffic, define rollback criteria, and preserve compatible configurations. Separate content drift from infrastructure faults so corrective actions target the actual cause.
articles.boundary: Monitoring only successful HTTP responses misses unsupported answers and broken evidence. Content logging must respect privacy and access controls.
articles.example: A prompt release is canaried and rolled back when supported-answer quality falls despite stable API latency.
articles.application: Operating changing GenAI services with measurable release risk.

articles.title: Latency, token cost and caching
articles.concept: GenAI cost and latency depend on prompt length, generated length, model choice, concurrency, and caching. Optimize against an explicit quality target rather than minimizing one metric in isolation.
articles.mechanism: Measure queue time, retrieval time, prefill, time to first token, and decode rate separately. Budget input and output tokens, remove redundant evidence, and compare routing or caching strategies on representative traffic. Include cache misses and invalidation behavior, and compute cost from actual metered units and current configured prices.
articles.boundary: Caching can serve stale or unauthorized content when keys omit revision or permission scope. Faster responses are not useful if answer quality drops below requirements.
articles.example: A support assistant shortens redundant context and bounds output while retaining required citations.
articles.application: Cost-aware interactive systems with service-level latency and quality objectives.

articles.title: GPU inference, batching and KV memory
articles.concept: GPU inference performance depends on model weights, activations, KV cache, memory bandwidth, and scheduling. Different request phases stress hardware differently.
articles.mechanism: Prefill processes prompt tokens and builds state, while decoding produces tokens incrementally using cached keys and values. Estimate memory for weights and KV cache separately, measure realistic context and concurrency, and evaluate batching policies. Track queue delay and tail latency because maximizing throughput can reduce interactive responsiveness.
articles.boundary: Checkpoint size alone is not the runtime memory requirement. KV cache scales with sequence length and active requests, and architecture changes such as grouped-query attention affect its size.
articles.example: A serving team bounds long contexts to prevent one batch from exhausting memory for other users.
articles.application: Capacity planning and efficient self-hosted language-model serving.

articles.title: Docker, Kubernetes and cloud deployment
articles.concept: Containers package an application runtime, while orchestration manages replicas, networking, rollout, and recovery. Successful deployment also requires model readiness, secrets, and external dependencies.
articles.mechanism: Build reproducible images, run with minimal privileges, configure health and readiness separately, and inject secrets through approved runtime mechanisms. Set resource requests and limits, handle termination gracefully, and roll out compatible configuration versions. Test dependency failures and cold starts before promising availability.
articles.boundary: A running container is not necessarily ready to serve model requests. GPU scheduling and memory requirements need explicit configuration and measurement.
articles.example: A new replica loads its model before readiness passes, preventing traffic from reaching an incomplete startup.
articles.application: Repeatable deployment of API and inference services on cloud infrastructure.

articles.title: Production debugging and MNC mock interviews
articles.concept: Production debugging starts with a reproducible symptom, bounded impact, and evidence. Interview preparation should demonstrate reasoning and truthful engineering ownership rather than memorized claims.
articles.mechanism: Establish the incident timeline, scope affected users, compare recent changes, and inspect correlated stage metrics. Mitigate safely before pursuing a complete root cause, preserve relevant evidence with privacy controls, and verify recovery using user-facing outcomes. Convert findings into tests, monitoring, and ownership changes, then explain tradeoffs in a structured project discussion.
articles.boundary: Correlation with a deployment is not proof of causation. Do not invent production experience or claim that original practice questions were asked by a company.
articles.example: A RAG incident is traced to a stale index activation pointer; rollback restores current evidence and a revision check prevents recurrence.
articles.application: Incident response, portfolio reviews, system-design discussions, and behavioral interviews.
